name: Calculate additive seasonal effects and adjusted values
subject: Statistics
description: In an additive model Y=T+S+R, a seasonal effect is measured in the original units and adjusted observations subtract that effect. A full cycle’s effects are centred around zero so they do not absorb the overall level.
learning_objectives: Use seasonal effects to adjust observations and reconstruct a fitted value.
understanding_evidence: Subtracts rather than divides in an additive model and keeps units.
common_misconceptions: Additive and multiplicative seasonal adjustment use the same calculation.

diagnostic_questions.question: Observed December sales are 260 and the additive December effect is +40. Find the seasonally adjusted value; if trend is 210, find residual.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: Removing the seasonal lift isolates level plus residual; the remaining 10 is unexplained by the fitted model.
hints: Write Y=T+S+R.
Remove S from Y, then compare with T.

applicability.notes: Editorial diagnostic placement. Apply the specific curriculum-mapping scope before choosing a question; a diagnostic is not official assessment evidence.

short_activity.instructions: Use four seasonal effects −20,0,+30,−10 to adjust a quarterly series and check that their sum is zero.

name: Areas under and between intersecting curves
subject: Mathematics
description: Area between two curves is the integral of upper minus lower over the relevant interval. If their ordering changes, split at intersection points; geometric area is non-negative even when a signed difference changes sign.
learning_objectives: Find bounds from intersections, choose curve order and calculate an enclosed area.
understanding_evidence: Solves the intersection equation and checks which curve is above on each interval.
common_misconceptions: Integrating the wrong order or allowing positive and negative areas to cancel.

diagnostic_questions.question: Find the area enclosed by y=2x and y=x².
diagnostic_questions.explanation: Intersections occur at x=0,2. The line is above the parabola between them, so ∫₀²(2x−x²)dx=[x²−x³/3]₀²=4/3.
hints: Find the intersections to determine the interval.
Test a point between the bounds to identify the upper curve.

applicability.notes: Editorial diagnostic placement. Apply the specific curriculum-mapping scope before choosing a question; a diagnostic is not official assessment evidence.

short_activity.instructions: Modify the interval so curves exchange order. Ask the learner to identify every required split and explain why one signed integral may undercount total area.

name: Average and instantaneous rates of change
subject: Mathematics
description: An average rate is a change in output divided by a non-zero input interval, represented by a secant slope. An instantaneous rate is the limiting local slope when it exists, represented by a tangent.

name: Use blocking or paired comparisons to manage experimental variation
subject: Statistics
description: Blocking groups units with similar relevant characteristics before random allocation within blocks. diagnostic_questions.explanation: Within-person comparison can reduce between-person variation, but an uncontrolled order can create a misleading effect.

name: Build a percentile bootstrap interval for a group difference
subject: Statistics
description: For two independent groups, resample within each group separately at its original size, calculate the chosen difference in a fixed order, and repeat. Percentiles of the bootstrap differences give a percentile interval; its actual coverage depends on sample quality, size and statistic.

common_misconceptions: Pool and shuffle groups to make a bootstrap confidence interval, or subtract two separate interval endpoints.

diagnostic_questions.explanation: The distribution contains repeated estimates of one difference. Pooling and shuffling instead imposes a no-group-link model used in randomisation testing.

name: Construct a bootstrap resample from observed data
subject: Statistics
description: A basic nonparametric bootstrap treats the empirical sample as a model of the population and draws with replacement, keeping the original sample size. Repeating the statistic estimates its sampling variation; it cannot repair a biased original sample.
learning_objectives: Create a valid resample and explain why replacement is essential.
understanding_evidence: Allows repeats and omissions while preserving n and the original measurement units.
common_misconceptions: A bootstrap resample is a new independent population sample, or sampling without replacement is equivalent.

diagnostic_questions.question: Original values are [2,4,7,9]. Is [4,4,9,2] a valid bootstrap resample? Is drawing all four once without replacement useful for varying their mean?
diagnostic_questions.answer: The first is valid. Drawing all four without replacement only reorders the same data, so its mean does not vary.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: Replacement lets observed values recur and others be absent, reproducing an estimated form of sample-to-sample variation.
hints: Check where values may be drawn from and how many draws are made.

name: Forward and backward passes in critical path analysis
subject: Mathematics
description: A forward pass computes earliest times using the latest required predecessor finish. A backward pass from project completion computes latest allowed times using the earliest successor deadline.
learning_objectives: Calculate earliest and latest starts/finishes and identify the project duration.
understanding_evidence: Takes a maximum at a forward merge and a minimum during the backward pass.
common_misconceptions: Taking the shortest incoming route at a merge when all predecessors must finish.

diagnostic_questions.question: Use A=3 h, B=4 h after A, C=2 h after A, D=1 h after B and C. Find the earliest completion and critical path. For a completion deadline of 8 h, what is C’s latest start and total float?
diagnostic_questions.answer: Earliest completion 8 h; critical path A–B–D. C’s latest start is 5 h and its total float is 2 h.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: Forward: A finishes at 3, B at 7, C at 5; D starts at max(7,5)=7 and finishes at 8. Backward: D must start at 8−1=7, so C must finish by 7 and may start at 7−2=5. Since C’s earliest start is 3, its total float is 5−3=2. With several successors, use the minimum of their latest starts as a task’s latest finish.
hints: Calculate earliest finishes forward; at a merge take the latest required predecessor finish.
Work backward from the deadline. Subtract D’s duration, then C’s duration; compare C’s latest start with its earliest start.

name: The derivative from first principles
subject: Mathematics
description: At a point a, the derivative is the limit of [f(a+h)−f(a)]/h as non-zero h tends to zero, when that limit exists. Algebra removes the apparent zero-over-zero form before the limiting step.

name: Draw a contextual conclusion from an interval for a difference

description: The position of an interval relative to zero provides evidence about direction of a population difference. An interval spanning zero leaves both signs compatible; an interval entirely away from zero can still represent a practically small difference.

diagnostic_questions.explanation: Zero and both signs lie within the interval, so the procedure cannot distinguish a directional difference reliably here.

name: Divisibility tests in base ten
subject: Mathematics
description: Base-ten place value allows exact divisibility decisions without full division. Tests use the final digit for 2,5,10; the final two digits for 4; final three digits for 8; and digit sums for 3 or 9. Divisibility by 6 requires both 2 and 3.
learning_objectives: Choose and apply divisibility tests for 2,3,4,5,6,8,9 and 10, including explaining a combined test.
understanding_evidence: Can justify this reasoning: The final digit is even; the digit sum is 12, so 3 divides but 9 does not. The final two digits 24 are divisible by 4, and 624=8×78. Both 2 and 3 divide, so 6 divides; the final digit excludes 5 and 10.
common_misconceptions: A digit sum divisible by 3 automatically proves divisibility by 9, or divisibility by either 2 or 3 alone proves divisibility by 6.

diagnostic_questions.question: Which of 2,3,4,5,6,8,9 and 10 divide 624 exactly? Explain the tests for 6 and 9.
diagnostic_questions.answer: 2,3,4,6 and 8 divide 624. The numbers 5,9 and 10 do not.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: The final digit is even; the digit sum is 12, so 3 divides but 9 does not. The final two digits 24 are divisible by 4, and 624=8×78. Both 2 and 3 divide, so 6 divides; the final digit excludes 5 and 10.
hints: Group the divisors by whether their test uses an ending or a digit sum.
For 6, check two necessary conditions together. For 9, test the digit sum against nine itself.

applicability.notes: Editorial diagnostic placement. Apply the specific curriculum-mapping scope before choosing a question; a diagnostic is not official assessment evidence.

short_activity.instructions: Choose a three-digit number and record eight yes/no predictions. Check only the surprising decisions with multiplication, then explain one test from place value.

name: Why division by zero is undefined
subject: Mathematics
description: Division reverses multiplication only when the divisor is nonzero. A nonzero number divided by zero has no possible quotient; zero divided by zero does not determine a unique quotient.
learning_objectives: Distinguish zero divided by a positive number from division by zero and explain using multiplication.
understanding_evidence: Can justify this reasoning: Six equal shares of zero each contain zero. For 6÷0 a quotient q would need 0×q=6, but multiplication by zero always gives zero.
Can justify this reasoning: For nonzero divisors multiplication determines one quotient; here all numbers would pass the check, so ordinary division is not defined.
common_misconceptions: Any division with a zero in it equals zero, or division by zero produces an ordinary very large number.

diagnostic_questions.explanation: Six equal shares of zero each contain zero. For 6÷0 a quotient q would need 0×q=6, but multiplication by zero always gives zero.
hints: Reverse each proposed division into a multiplication statement.

name: Construct an informal interval for a population median
subject: Statistics
description: One senior teaching method estimates a population median using sample median ± 1.5×IQR/√n. It is an informal method with context-dependent performance, distinct from a bootstrap interval or a guaranteed 95% interval.
learning_objectives: Calculate an informal interval and explain how n and spread affect width.
understanding_evidence: Uses the smaller sample’s own n and IQR for its own interval.
common_misconceptions: This informal interval contains 95% of the individual observations.

diagnostic_questions.question: A sample median is 24 min, IQR is 10 min and n=100. Find the informal interval.
diagnostic_questions.answer: 24±1.5×10/√100 = 24±1.5, giving 22.5 to 25.5 min for the population median.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: The interval estimates a median, not the spread of travellers’ individual times.
hints: Find √n first.
Calculate the margin and add/subtract it from the sample median.

short_activity.instructions: Keep the median and IQR fixed and compare intervals for n=25 and n=100; explain the factor-of-two change.

name: Integer exponent laws

name: Kinematics: displacement and total distance by integration

name: Inverse functions and domain restriction
subject: Mathematics

name: Distinguishing inverse and reciprocal functions
subject: Mathematics
description: An inverse reverses an input-output mapping, whereas a reciprocal replaces each non-zero output by its multiplicative inverse. These operations produce different formulas, domains and graph relationships.
learning_objectives: Compare f⁻¹(x) and 1/f(x) algebraically and graphically.
understanding_evidence: Uses function reversal for f⁻¹ and denominator restrictions for 1/f.
common_misconceptions: Interpreting the −1 superscript on an inverse function as ordinary exponent −1.

diagnostic_questions.question: For f(x)=2x+3, give f⁻¹(x) and 1/f(x), with domains.

diagnostic_questions.explanation: The inverse solves y=2x+3 for the old input. The reciprocal retains the input and reciprocates its output.

name: Investigate experimental probabilities in a multi-stage trial
subject: Statistics
description: A multi-stage probability enquiry defines a complete trial, collects repeated outcomes and interprets the observed distribution. Relative frequency divides successes by complete trials, and a model comparison requires stated assumptions.

understanding_evidence: Counts each complete trial once and distinguishes observed from theoretical probability.
common_misconceptions: Divide successes by the number of possible outcomes rather than the number of trials.

diagnostic_questions.question: In 200 simulated trials, two fair dice are rolled and their sum recorded; 31 sums are 7. Find the observed estimate and theoretical comparison.

diagnostic_questions.explanation: One trial includes both rolls. Differences between frequencies and the model are expected in finite samples.
hints: What exactly happens in one full trial?
Count favourable pairs separately from the 200 observed trials.

name: Choose a sample-size-appropriate visual population comparison
subject: Statistics
description: Level 1 visual inference considers random sampling, separation, overlap, overall spread and the smaller group size. The 2026 guidance uses non-overlapping middle halves, a clear 75%-to-50% comparison for samples of 20–40, and relative median separation for large samples of at least 100. These are contextual heuristics, not universal significance tests.
learning_objectives: Use the appropriate visual evidence and avoid extending a sample statement to a population without a defensible sample.
understanding_evidence: Uses the smaller n and acknowledges when the guidance does not settle a borderline case.
common_misconceptions: A visible median difference proves a population difference for any sample size.

diagnostic_questions.question: Group A has n=120 and group B n=25, both random samples. May the large-sample visual rule be justified solely by A having 120?
diagnostic_questions.answer: No. Use the smaller sample size, 25, and assess the appropriate small-sample visual separation and context; the larger group alone does not justify the large-sample rule.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: The less precisely represented group still limits a comparison. The guidance provides specific visual reasoning, not a formal confidence interval.
hints: Identify the smaller sample.
Check the guidance for that sample-size range and examine overlap.

applicability.notes: Editorial diagnostic placement. Apply the specific curriculum-mapping scope before choosing a question; a diagnostic is not official assessment evidence.

name: Interpreting linear programming edge cases
subject: Mathematics
description: A linear programme can have no feasible solution, an unbounded objective or many optimal solutions. Whole-number decisions require a justified search or bound over feasible integer points. Rounding a continuous optimum may violate constraints or miss the best integer solution; checking only a few nearby points is not generally sufficient.
learning_objectives: Recognise non-unique, infeasible and unbounded cases and test integer feasibility.
understanding_evidence: Explains which constraint or objective direction causes the case, with a specific feasible example or contradiction.
common_misconceptions: Assuming every problem has one optimal vertex, or rounding a continuous optimum without checking constraints.

diagnostic_questions.question: Maximise x+y with x≥0, y≥0 and x+y≤4. Is the optimal point unique?
diagnostic_questions.answer: No. Every point on x+y=4 with 0≤x≤4 is optimal, with value 4.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: The objective is parallel to and coincides with the active boundary at its maximum.
hints: Evaluate the objective at both endpoints of the sloping boundary.
Check what value the objective has at any point between those endpoints.

applicability.notes: Editorial diagnostic placement. Apply the specific curriculum-mapping scope before choosing a question; a diagnostic is not official assessment evidence.

diagnostic_questions.question: Maximise 3x+2y for non-negative integers x,y subject to 2x+y≤5 and x+2y≤5. The continuous intersection is (5/3,5/3). Can it be rounded to (2,2), and what is the integer optimum?
diagnostic_questions.answer: (2,2) is infeasible because both left sides become 6>5. The integer optimum is (2,1), with objective value 8.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: The constraints imply integer x=0,1,2. Their largest feasible integer y values are respectively 2,2,1; since the objective increases with y, the best values for those x are 4,7,8. This exhaustive reduced search proves the maximum.
hints: Test a proposed rounded point in every constraint.
Bound the possible integer x values, then choose the largest allowed integer y for each because its objective coefficient is positive.

name: Unique, inconsistent and dependent linear systems
subject: Mathematics
description: Elimination may lead to a unique solution, a contradiction such as 0=5, or a redundant statement 0=0. A redundant equation signals dependency but the remaining equations must still be checked for consistency and free variables.
learning_objectives: Classify a linear system using elimination and express a family of solutions parametrically.

diagnostic_questions.question: Classify the system x+y+z=3, 2x+2y+2z=6, x−y=1 and describe its solutions. What changes if the second right side is 7?

diagnostic_questions.explanation: The second equation repeats twice the first. Set y=t; then x=t+1 and z=2−2t. Replacing 6 by 7 produces the contradiction 0=1 after elimination.
hints: Subtract twice the first equation from the second.

description: A network represents objects or events as vertices and connections as edges or directed arcs. Weights can represent distance, time or cost, while connectivity does not depend on the drawing scale.
learning_objectives: Translate a situation into a labelled weighted network and interpret a route.
understanding_evidence: Distinguishes vertex, edge, weight and direction and does not infer missing connections from crossing lines.
common_misconceptions: Treating the visual length of an edge as its weight or assuming every crossing is a vertex.

diagnostic_questions.question: A connects to B with weight 4, B to C with 3, and A to C with 10. What is the weight of route A–B–C?
diagnostic_questions.explanation: A route cost adds the weights of the traversed edges: 4+3, rather than using the direct A–C edge.
hints: List the edges actually used by the route.
Add their labels, not the distances measured in the drawing.

name: Euler trails and network traversability
subject: Mathematics
description: An Euler trail traverses each edge exactly once. In a connected undirected network with at least one edge, such a trail exists when there are zero or two odd-degree vertices; zero odd vertices permit a closed Euler circuit.
learning_objectives: Test whether a connected undirected network can be traversed once per edge and identify allowed endpoints.
understanding_evidence: Counts edge degrees, checks connectivity and distinguishes an edge-once trail from a vertex-once route.
common_misconceptions: Using the criterion for disconnected networks or confusing Euler trails with Hamiltonian paths.

diagnostic_questions.question: A connected network has vertex degrees 3,3,2,2. Can it have an Euler trail and a closed Euler circuit?
diagnostic_questions.answer: It can have an open Euler trail between the two degree-3 vertices, but no closed Euler circuit.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: Exactly two vertices have odd degree. Internal visits pair entry and exit edges, leaving an unpaired edge at each endpoint.
hints: Count how many vertices have odd degree.
For every internal visit, pair the entering and leaving edge; only endpoints can be unpaired.

applicability.notes: Editorial diagnostic placement. Apply the specific curriculum-mapping scope before choosing a question; a diagnostic is not official assessment evidence.

short_activity.instructions: Draw a simple network with two odd vertices and trace each edge once. Add one edge between the odd vertices and explain the change in traversability.

name: Modelling change towards an equilibrium
subject: Mathematics
description: A rate proportional to the difference from equilibrium is dT/dt=−k(T−Tₐ), k>0, giving T=Tₐ+(T₀−Tₐ)e⁻ᵏᵗ. In Newton’s cooling model, Tₐ is constant ambient temperature, not zero by default.
learning_objectives: Form and solve a simple equilibrium-approach model and estimate a parameter from observations.
understanding_evidence: Models excess above equilibrium and checks that the solution approaches the ambient value.
common_misconceptions: Using T₀e⁻ᵏᵗ when the limiting temperature is not zero.

diagnostic_questions.question: A drink starts at 80°C in a constant 20°C room; after 10 minutes it is 50°C. Give T(t) under Newton’s cooling model.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: The excess temperature falls from 60 to 30 in 10 minutes, so its decay constant is ln2/10.
hints: Work with temperature above the room temperature.
Use the observed halving of that excess to determine k.

name: Choose a nonlinear statistical model and interpret transformed predictions
subject: Statistics
description: Curved relationships may need a nonlinear model or a justified transformation. Model choice should combine pattern, residual checks and context; predictions on a transformed scale must be returned to the original scale with care. learning_objectives: Explain why a line is inadequate and interpret a simple transformed fitted model.
understanding_evidence: Back-transforms correctly and does not assume the transformed fit proves a causal law.
common_misconceptions: A straight line is always best, or a prediction for log(y) is already a prediction in y units.

diagnostic_questions.explanation: The logarithm must be inverted. This is the model’s fitted value, not automatically an unbiased estimate of the arithmetic conditional mean.

name: Compare an empirical distribution with a normal model
subject: Statistics
description: A normal curve is a model, not a guarantee about a measured population. Shape, impossible values, tail behaviour and observed interval proportions help judge whether its use is reasonable for the intended question.
learning_objectives: Compare model predictions with observed data and identify a meaningful limitation.
understanding_evidence: Uses a specific distribution feature rather than assuming all measurements are normal.
common_misconceptions: Knowing mean and SD proves normality.

diagnostic_questions.explanation: Two moments do not determine the full shape of a distribution.

name: Recover a normal-model parameter from a percentile
subject: Statistics
description: A known percentile gives a standardised equation x=μ+zσ. It can determine a missing mean or SD when the remaining information is sufficient; two independent percentile equations can determine both. Parameter values should be checked against the original probabilities and context.
learning_objectives: Rearrange a percentile equation to recover a plausible model parameter.
understanding_evidence: Uses a positive SD and the appropriate signed z value.
common_misconceptions: An upper percentile has a negative z value, or a probability can be substituted directly for z.

diagnostic_questions.question: A normal model has mean 60. Its percentile corresponding to z=2 is 68. Find σ and explain why σ cannot be −4.
diagnostic_questions.answer: 68=60+2σ, so σ=4. Standard deviation measures spread and is non-negative; here positive spread is required.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: The z value is a number of SDs from the mean, not the percentile probability itself.
hints: Write x=μ+zσ.
Subtract μ and divide by z, then check the sign and units.

applicability.notes: Editorial diagnostic placement. Apply the specific curriculum-mapping scope before choosing a question; a diagnostic is not official assessment evidence.

short_activity.instructions: Use two supplied percentile points to set up two equations for μ and σ and verify the resulting model.

name: Estimating derivatives numerically

name: Parabolas as focus-directrix loci
subject: Mathematics
description: A parabola consists of points equidistant from a focus and a directrix. In (x−h)²=4p(y−k), its vertex is (h,k), focus (h,k+p), and directrix y=k−p; horizontal forms exchange x and y.
learning_objectives: Connect a parabola equation with its focus, directrix, vertex and orientation.
understanding_evidence: Identifies signed p and uses equal distances to verify a point on the locus.
common_misconceptions: Using p=the coefficient 4p or placing the directrix through the vertex.

diagnostic_questions.question: For x²=8y, find the vertex, focus and directrix.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: Comparison with x²=4py gives p=2, so the focus is 2 units above the vertex and the directrix 2 below.
hints: Compare with the standard form x²=4py.
The focus and directrix lie the same distance from the vertex on opposite sides.

name: Infer a Poisson mean from an event probability
subject: Statistics
description: An observed or specified event probability can determine a Poisson parameter under the model. For no events, P(X=0)=e^(−λ), so λ=−ln P(X=0); more complex inverse questions can use numerical solving, with rates converted to the stated exposure.
learning_objectives: Recover λ from a zero-count probability and check units.
understanding_evidence: Uses the logarithm with the correct sign and distinguishes an estimated rate from an exact process law.
common_misconceptions: The probability of zero events is λ itself, or λ may be negative.

diagnostic_questions.question: A suitable Poisson model gives P(no calls in 30 minutes)=0.20. Find its expected calls per 30 minutes and hourly rate.
diagnostic_questions.answer: λ=−ln(0.20)≈1.609 per 30 minutes; hourly rate≈3.219 calls per hour.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: The parameter is the mean count in the model’s exposure. Doubling the exposure doubles the mean under a constant rate.
hints: Use P(X=0)=e^(−λ).
Take natural logs, change the sign, then scale the time interval.

applicability.notes: Editorial diagnostic placement. Apply the specific curriculum-mapping scope before choosing a question; a diagnostic is not official assessment evidence.

short_activity.instructions: Substitute the inferred λ back into the zero-count formula and discuss why an empirical estimate of 0.20 adds estimation uncertainty.

name: Use the approximate margin for independent polling groups
subject: Statistics
description: For a difference between independent polling groups, the taught approximate rule uses 1.5 times the average of their margins of error. This is a practical heuristic, not an exact formula; markedly unequal sample precision needs a properly justified combination method.

diagnostic_questions.explanation: The two estimates come from separate samples. The given classroom rule approximates combined uncertainty for this balanced case.
hints: Calculate each single-poll margin.

name: Distinguish independence from mutual exclusivity
subject: Statistics
description: Independence means learning one event occurred does not change the other event’s probability; equivalently P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). Mutual exclusivity means A∩B is empty, which implies P(A∩B)=0; probability zero alone need not mean an empty event in a continuous model. Positive-probability exclusive events cannot be independent.
learning_objectives: Test both properties using numerical evidence and explain their meanings.
understanding_evidence: Applies the product test rather than testing whether overlap is zero for independence.
common_misconceptions: Independent means the events cannot occur together.

diagnostic_questions.question: P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5, P(A∩B)=0.2. Are the events independent or mutually exclusive?
diagnostic_questions.answer: Independent because 0.2=0.4×0.5; not mutually exclusive because the intersection is positive.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: Independence permits overlap in the expected product proportion.
hints: Calculate the product of the two marginal probabilities.
Compare the intersection separately with the product and with zero.

applicability.notes: Editorial diagnostic placement. Apply the specific curriculum-mapping scope before choosing a question; a diagnostic is not official assessment evidence.

short_activity.instructions: Construct one independent and one mutually exclusive example and label the different tests.

name: Calculate and interpret risk and relative risk
subject: Statistics
description: Risk is an event proportion within a defined group. Relative risk divides two risks in a stated order; a ratio below one indicates lower risk and does not by itself establish causation.
learning_objectives: Calculate risks and compare them using unambiguous language.
understanding_evidence: States the reference group and interprets ratios above and below one.
common_misconceptions: Twice as likely means two percentage points higher, or a relative risk proves cause.

diagnostic_questions.question: Late rates are 12/40 for bus users and 8/60 for others. Find the relative risk for bus users compared with others.
diagnostic_questions.answer: (12/40)/(8/60)=2.25. In these data, bus users are 2.25 times as likely to be late; the absolute difference is about 16.7 percentage points.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: The ratio compares risks, whereas subtraction compares percentage points.
hints: Compute each group’s risk separately.
Divide in the order stated by the question.

name: Separate underlying probability, model and empirical estimates
subject: Statistics
description: An underlying chance mechanism has probabilities that may be unknown. A model assigns probabilities using assumptions; empirical estimates use observed outcomes. Neither estimated route automatically becomes exact by being expressed as a formula.

diagnostic_questions.explanation: The number of faces alone does not establish fairness.
hints: Ask whether each number comes from data or assumptions.
Check whether those assumptions match this die.

name: Translate survey purpose into information needs
subject: Statistics
description: Questionnaire design starts with the decisions its users need to make. Each question should produce a variable that helps answer the research purpose with an appropriate response format.

name: Randomly allocate experimental units to treatments
subject: Statistics
description: Random allocation assigns treatments by a chance mechanism so treatment labels are not chosen from unit characteristics. It protects against systematic allocation bias and supports causal comparison under a suitable design; it does not guarantee exact balance or population representativeness.
learning_objectives: Specify a reproducible allocation procedure and explain its purpose.
understanding_evidence: Uses a shuffled assignment or random number rule and distinguishes it from random sampling.
common_misconceptions: Random allocation guarantees identical groups or means the volunteers represent everyone.

diagnostic_questions.question: Twenty volunteers test two paper-plane designs. Why shuffle ten A and ten B assignments instead of letting confident throwers choose A?
diagnostic_questions.answer: Chance allocation reduces systematic connection between prior throwing ability and design. Self-selection could confound ability with design; random assignment does not ensure perfect realised balance.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: The treatment comparison should not be determined by a pre-existing characteristic affecting the response.
hints: Identify a characteristic that could influence flight distance.
Make treatment assignment independent of that characteristic by design.

applicability.notes: Editorial diagnostic placement. Apply the specific curriculum-mapping scope before choosing a question; a diagnostic is not official assessment evidence.

short_activity.instructions: Create an allocation list for 20 anonymous units using a reproducible spreadsheet shuffle and record the exact procedure.

name: Reason about random sequences without the gambler’s fallacy
subject: Statistics
description: Under independent trials with a fixed success probability, earlier outcomes do not change the next trial’s chance. Long-run stabilisation of relative frequency does not require an immediate compensating outcome.
learning_objectives: Explain streaks and distinguish independence assumptions from guaranteed balancing.
understanding_evidence: Keeps the next-trial probability fixed while acknowledging the process might be dependent in reality.
common_misconceptions: After many heads a tail becomes due.

diagnostic_questions.question: A fair coin gives HHHHH. If tosses are independent, what is P(head next), and must the next five tosses all be tails?
diagnostic_questions.answer: P(head next)=1/2; no compensation is required.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: Independence fixes each next-toss chance. Long-run proportions can stabilise without correcting every short-run imbalance.
hints: Separate the next toss from the long-run proportion.
Ask what independence says about information from earlier tosses.

applicability.notes: Editorial diagnostic placement. Apply the specific curriculum-mapping scope before choosing a question; a diagnostic is not official assessment evidence.

short_activity.instructions: Generate 40 tosses digitally, mark streaks and discuss why random data need not alternate.

name: Calculate expected value and net payoff
subject: Statistics
description: Expected value E(X)=ΣxP(X=x) is a probability-weighted long-run mean. It need not be a possible single outcome, and net payoff subtracts costs from receipts.
learning_objectives: Calculate expected value and interpret a decision in repeated-play terms.
understanding_evidence: Uses probability weights and distinguishes expected receipts from profit.
common_misconceptions: The expected value must occur on one trial, or a positive prize expectation guarantees profit.

diagnostic_questions.question: A game pays $0 with probability 0.7 and $10 with probability 0.3. Entry costs $4. Find expected net payoff.
diagnostic_questions.answer: Expected receipt=$3; expected net payoff=$3−$4=−$1 per play.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: A weighted average describes repeated outcomes, not a guaranteed result of any one game.
hints: Compute the mean receipt using the two probabilities.
Subtract the entry cost once per play.

name: Transform a random variable’s mean and standard deviation
subject: Statistics
description: For Y=a+bX, E(Y)=a+bE(X) and SD(Y)=|b|SD(X). Adding a constant shifts location without changing spread; scaling changes SD by absolute scale and variance by its square.

diagnostic_questions.explanation: The negative scale reverses order but still stretches distances by a factor of 2; the shift does not affect distances.

name: Compute variance and SD of a discrete random variable
subject: Statistics

name: Build a randomisation distribution under no treatment effect
subject: Statistics
description: Under the sharp null that treatment changes no individual unit’s outcome in a completely randomised experiment, outcomes can be reassigned among treatment labels using the original allocation scheme. Recomputing the statistic produces a distribution of effects due to random allocation alone; blocked or paired designs require constrained reassignment.
learning_objectives: Specify which labels are shuffled and what remains fixed under the null.
understanding_evidence: Preserves group sizes and distinguishes label permutation from within-group bootstrap resampling.
common_misconceptions: Randomisation testing draws outcomes with replacement separately within treatment groups.

diagnostic_questions.question: An experiment assigns 6 units to A and 6 to B. How would one null randomisation replicate be formed for a mean difference?
diagnostic_questions.answer: Pool the 12 observed outcomes, randomly allocate 6 to A and 6 to B following the original design, and calculate mean A−mean B. Repeat to represent allocation variation under no effect.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: The null removes association with treatment labels while retaining the observed outcomes and allocation constraints.
hints: State the no-effect assumption.
Shuffle labels, not new independently generated outcome values.

applicability.notes: Editorial diagnostic placement. Apply the specific curriculum-mapping scope before choosing a question; a diagnostic is not official assessment evidence.

short_activity.instructions: Use 12 labelled outcome cards to make several null allocations and plot the resulting differences.

name: Interpret tail evidence from a randomisation test
subject: Statistics
description: A randomisation tail proportion counts statistics at least as extreme as the observed statistic under the specified null model. Direction and two-sidedness must match the question; a small proportion is evidence against that null, not the probability the null is true.
learning_objectives: Calculate a simulated tail proportion and state a cautious contextual conclusion.
understanding_evidence: Includes both tails for a two-sided question and avoids a posterior-probability interpretation.
common_misconceptions: A p-value of 0.02 means a 2% probability of no effect or a 98% probability of causation.

diagnostic_questions.question: The observed A−B mean difference is 5. In 1000 null allocations, 18 differences have absolute value at least 5. Estimate the two-sided tail proportion and interpret.
diagnostic_questions.answer: 18/1000=0.018. Differences at least this far from zero were uncommon under the no-effect allocation model, providing evidence of a treatment effect if the design and measurement assumptions hold.
diagnostic_questions.explanation: The probability is conditional on the null model. It does not assign a probability to the null itself, and finite simulation adds numerical uncertainty.
hints: Identify the absolute-distance criterion for two tails.
Divide the qualifying replicates by the total and phrase the result under the null.

applicability.notes: Editorial diagnostic placement. Apply the specific curriculum-mapping scope before choosing a question; a diagnostic is not official assessment evidence.

short_activity.instructions: Compare one-sided and two-sided counts on a supplied null plot and explain why the scientific question must fix the choice.

name: Manipulating rational algebraic expressions

name: Converting a recurring decimal to a fraction

diagnostic_questions.explanation: 100x=27.272727…; subtracting x gives 99x=27. Thus x=27/99=3/11. The unending positive tail makes x greater than 0.27.

name: Solving separable differential equations

description: A separable equation y′=f(x)g(y) can be rearranged to dy/g(y)=f(x)dx where division is valid, then integrated. Constant solutions lost by dividing by g(y) must be checked separately.

name: Stacked bar graphs for paired categorical data
subject: Statistics
description: A stacked bar joins category-frequency segments into one total for each group. A segment’s frequency is its length, found by subtracting its lower endpoint from its upper endpoint; its top alone gives a cumulative total.

understanding_evidence: Can justify this reasoning: Each total adds both category counts. The upper banana segment has length8−4=4; its top value8 includes the apple count below it.
common_misconceptions: Read a top segment’s cumulative endpoint as that category’s count, or treat unequal-total absolute bars as if they were already100%-scaled bars.

diagnostic_questions.question: Group A has3 apple choices and2 banana choices; Group B has4 apple choices and4 banana choices. Apples are the bottom segments of a stacked bar graph. What are the total bar heights, and what count is represented by B’s banana segment from4 to8?

diagnostic_questions.explanation: Each total adds both category counts. The upper banana segment has length8−4=4; its top value8 includes the apple count below it.

name: Use standard error to describe uncertainty in a sample mean
subject: Statistics
description: For independent observations with population SD σ, the SD of the sample mean is σ/√n; s/√n estimates it. Standard error describes variation of a statistic across samples, while sample SD describes variation among observations.

diagnostic_questions.explanation: The mean of 64 observations varies less across samples than individual measurements do.
